before.title: A/C Condenser Leaks (Road-Debris Damage, Exposed Front Mounting)
before.description: The Juke's air-conditioning condenser sits low and exposed at the front of the vehicle, making it prone to punctures from rocks and road debris and to fin/seal corrosion. Once it leaks refrigerant, the A/C blows warm and the system loses charge. Because the tubes and seals can't be repaired individually, a full condenser replacement is required. This is wear/damage-driven, not a factory recall or TSB.
before.solution: Perform a leak inspection (dye/UV), then replace the A/C condenser, evacuate and recharge the system. A protective grille/mesh can reduce future debris strikes.
symptoms: A/C blows warm air
Refrigerant loss / needs frequent recharge
Visible oily/green residue on the condenser
Bent or damaged condenser fins

before.title: CVT Transmission Failure (Jatco CVT7)
before.description: The Juke CVT (Jatco CVT7/JF015E) paired with the turbocharged engine is stressed beyond its design capacity. The turbo's torque output accelerates CVT wear, leading to shuddering, slipping, and failure often before 100,000 miles. AWD models add additional strain on the CVT.
before.solution: Change CVT fluid every 25,000 miles with NS-3 (more frequent than standard due to turbo stress). Avoid launching the vehicle aggressively. CVT replacement costs $3,500-5,000. Check extended warranty eligibility.
symptoms: Shuddering during acceleration
CVT slipping under boost
Whining noise from transmission
Loss of drive at highway speeds
Transmission overheating warning

communityRecommendations.text: Change CVT fluid every 25k miles, not 30k - the turbo puts extra stress on the CVT

communityRecommendations.content: CVT fluid specifically formulated for continuous variable transmissions

before.title: Engine Start/Stop Push-Button Sticks, Causing Unexpected Shutoff (Recall 15V418)
before.description: On 2013-2014 Jukes built July 3 - October 22, 2013, the engine start/stop button can stick inside its housing when exposed to hot temperatures. If it stays depressed, normal road vibration can register a shutdown request and switch the engine off while driving, causing a stall and loss of power assist.
before.solution: Under NHTSA recall 15V418000, dealers modify the start/stop switch housing free of charge. Out of warranty, the remedy is replacing the ignition push-button switch assembly.
symptoms: Engine shuts off unexpectedly while driving
Push-button start sticks or feels jammed
Intermittent failure to start
Stalling more likely in hot weather

before.title: Fuel Pressure Sensor Loosens and Leaks Fuel (Recall 14V683 / PC618)
before.description: The fuel pressure sensor threaded into the high-pressure fuel line on the MR16DDT engine was not sufficiently torqued at the factory, so it can loosen with vehicle usage and cause a fuel leak. A fuel leak in the presence of an ignition source could cause an under-hood fire. Nissan issued multiple related campaigns (early 12V069, PC618, and expanded recall 14V683) covering 2011-2014 Jukes.
before.solution: Under recall, dealers re-torque (and on some VINs replace) the fuel pressure sensor at no cost. Out of warranty, the fix is to re-torque or replace the sensor and confirm no fuel weeping.
symptoms: Strong raw fuel/gasoline smell
Visible fuel seepage or drips near the fuel rail
Fuel odor after driving or when parked
Possible check-engine light

before.title: Timing Chain Stretch (MR16DDT Engine)
before.description: The Juke MR16DDT engine timing chain stretches prematurely, especially with irregular oil changes. The chain tensioner cannot compensate for excessive stretch, leading to timing issues and potential engine damage. This is more common in the turbo engine than in other Nissan 1.6L variants.
before.solution: Replace timing chain, tensioner, and guides. Use updated Nissan timing chain kit. Job costs $800-1,500 at an independent shop. Always use full synthetic oil and change every 5,000 miles to prevent recurrence.
symptoms: Rattling noise on startup
Check engine light with P0011/P0014
Rough idle
Poor acceleration
Engine misfires

before.title: Turbocharger Failure (MR16DDT Engine)
before.description: The Nissan Juke MR16DDT 1.6L turbo engine suffers from premature turbocharger failure. The turbo bearings wear out, causing oil consumption, smoke, and eventual boost loss. Loss of boost/power
Excessive oil consumption

before.title: Turbocharger Oil Feed Line Leak
before.description: The Juke's 1.6L turbocharged engine develops oil leaks from the turbo oil feed line and the turbo oil return gasket. The banjo bolt on the oil feed line can work loose, and the gasket where the oil returns to the engine block degrades from heat exposure. The leak drips onto the exhaust, creating smoke and a burning oil smell. If oil supply is restricted, the turbo bearing can fail.
before.solution: Re-torque the oil feed banjo bolt and replace the crush washers ($5 in parts). Replace the turbo oil return gasket ($10-$20). If the turbo is already damaged from oil starvation, a replacement turbo costs $800-$1,500. Use synthetic oil and change every 3,000-5,000 miles to maintain turbo health. Always idle the engine for 30-60 seconds before shutting off after spirited driving.
symptoms: Burning oil smell from engine bay
Smoke from turbo/exhaust area
Oil dripping onto exhaust heat shield
Low oil level between changes
Blue smoke on startup

citations.title: Nissan Technical Service Bulletin NTB11-065: Turbocharger Oil Leak Diagnosis and Repair

communityRecommendations.content: Check the turbo oil feed banjo bolt torque at every oil change. It loosens over time. A $5 set of copper crush washers and re-torque fixes the most common turbo oil leak on the Juke.
Turbo gasket kit prevents boost leaks and oil seepage at the turbo flanges
Boost gauge helps monitor turbo performance and catch problems early
